full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan J: This Criminal Miscellaneous Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure has arisen out of the judgment and order of conviction passed under section 25-B(1) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 sentencing the accused petitioner Sohail Ahmed Chowdhury to imprisonment for life with a fine of taka 5000.00, in default, to suffer RI for 1 (one) year more along with the confiscation of the seized article including the gold by the Special Tribunal Judge, Dhaka on 15.2.1988 in Special Tribunal Case No. 113 of 1986 arising out of Cantonment Police Station Case No. 15(3) 86. This miscellaneous case has a required history. Having been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life as mentioned above, the accused petitioner filed Criminal Appeal No. 713 of 1990 before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court which having been reported as time barred an application was filed for admission of appeal after condoning the delay caused in filing the appeal and a Rule was issued by this court on 3.9.90. The condonation matter being Criminal Revision No. 770(R) of 1990 was once heard by a Division Bench of this court but before its disposal the matter was sent to this Bench by the learned Chief Justice for hearing and disposal. As there is no scope for getting relief on the application filed under section 5 of the Limitation Act in respect of a time-barred appeal arising out of conviction and sentence passed under the Special Powers Act, instead of pressing the application for condonation of delay prayer was made on behalf of the accused petitioner for conversion of the Criminal Appeal No. 718 of 1990 along with the Criminal Revision No. 770(R) of 1990 to an application for quashment of the judgment and order of conviction and sentence invoking the aid of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the said prayer having been allowed after hearing the learned Advocate for the accused petitioner and the learned Attorney-General appearing along with the learned Deputy Attorney-General the application under section 561A CrPC was registered as Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 944 of 1995. In the above context the present Criminal Miscellaneous Case is directed against the judgment and order dated 15.2.88 passed against the accused petitioner under section 25-B of the Special Powers Act with a prayer for setting aside the order of conviction and sentence on quashment on the ground of patent illegalities in order to secure the ends of justice. 

 2. The prosecution case out of which the Criminal Miscellaneous Case has arisen are as follows: 

 The petitioner was the Junior Purser in Bangladesh Biman. On 13.3.86 at about 12-55 hours he came from Jeddah in Bangladesh Airlines Flight No. BG-038 and placed his baggage at the Customs Crew center for checking by surveillance team and it was found that there was a declaration for one old suitcase and a brief case but there was no declaration of wrist watches which were found in his possession. The accused-petitioner was taken to the chamber of Superintendent of Customs where on search several wrist watches, key rings were found in his possession and 12 gold bars were recovered from his anklet covered by black socks and adhesive tape. Each bar weighed 10(ten) tolas of gold and thus in total 240 tolas of gold was recovered and seized from the accused petitioner who having failed to produce any valid document in support of his possession of gold FIR was lodged and a case was started under section 156(8) of the Customs Act 1969 and 25-B of the Special Powers Act against the accused petitioner. The seized gold and other goods seized were, however, deposited with the godown-in-charge of Zia International Airport Customs, Dhaka. The police after investigation submitted charge-sheet against the accused petitioner under section 156(8) of the Customs Act and 25-B of the Special Powers Act. On transfer the trial was held in the Court of Special Tribunal, Anti-Smuggling Court Dhaka. The accused petitioner pleaded not guilty to the charge levelled against him. The further case of the defence was that he had been falsely implicated in the case out of previous enmity and grudge by the designing persons and neither any gold nor any contraband goods were recovered from him. 

 3. Mr. Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Advocate along with Advocate Farah Mahbub appeared for the accused petitioner and Mr. AFM Shahid, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appeared for the State. At the outset Mr. Mahbubur Rahman took us through the judgment of the trial Court and submitted that the conviction is based on no evidence and hence liable to be quashed to secure the ends of justice. It is submitted that in order to secure conviction of an accused on a charge for which deterrent punishment has been provided under the Special Powers' Act, as in the present case, the evidence must be conclusive and guilt must be proved beyond all reasonable doubt according to the principle of Criminal Jurisprudence. The learned Advocate then submitted that the learned trial Court based his decision on mere hypothesis and conjectures rather than on actual evidence on record in total ignorance of fundamental principle of criminal justice and in that view of the matter the judgment and order of conviction is liable to be set aside and quashed to secure the ends of justice. It is submitted that the prosecution case of recovery and seizure of the gold has been totally shaken due to the non-production of the seized gold in the court during trial for its identification by the PW s and examination of the court and non-production of the seized gold without furnishing any explanation by the prosecution has vitiated the trial. There is also no evidence that the gold alleged to have been recovered from the accused petitioner was ever tested by any chemical examiner/expert to prove that it was really gold. The person who is said to have weighed the gold has also not been examined in the case. These omissions, laches and lacunae being of vital nature have cast a serious doubt on the prosecution case and the learned trial Court tried to reconcile this vital defect of the prosecution and filled up the gap himself in arriving at the finding of guilt of the accused petitioner against the principle of criminal jurisprudence, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted. 

 4. Mr. AFM Shahid, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, submitted that the submission made on behalf of the accused petitioner may be good grounds of appeal but as it touches the merit of the case requiring reassessment and re-consideration of the evidence it is not within the scope of the High Court Division in its inherent jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 7. In the case of Vaketeswardev vs. State of Andhra Prodesh reported in AIR 1987 page 1621 it was held "High Court can exercise power to correct patent illegality and to secure the ends of justice and the only caution expressed is that it should be exercised sparingly and not arbitrarily. Moreover, the nature of offence has to be taken into consideration." In the case of Muleem Singh vs. State it was observed: "The inherent power is to be exercised to do the right and to undo a wrong in the cause of administration of justice and this power ought to be exercised sparingly only when the court feels that the ends of justice requires it and not as a matter of routine." In the case of Mofazzal Mollah and others vs. State reported in 45 DLR (AD) 175 the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court while setting aside the conviction allowing the appeal arising out of the order rejecting the application under section 561A of the Code observed: "In disposing of the application under section 561A CrPC the learned Judges of the High Court Division fell into the same error as the learned Sessions Judge and did not take into consideration whether the conviction was based on any legal evidence." In the said case Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ delivering the judgment observed "The learned Judges proceeded on the assumption that section 56lA CrPC is meant only for quashing a criminal proceeding before trial has started and when the trial, as in the present case, has been concluded, followed by an appeal and a revision both being unsuccessful how the convicted accused could come under this section for quashing the proceeding. Section 561A CrPC has only reiterated the court's inherent power to give effect to any order to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. In this case, the appellants invoked the inherent power of the court to secure the ends of justice by getting the order of their conviction quashed or set aside on the ground that the conviction was based on no evidence. The learned Judges failed to exercise their power under this section to look into the matter and see whether the conviction was valid and legal or whether it was invalid on the very face of it for want of any legal evidence to support it. The fact that the accused were tried and found guilty and then unsuccessfully filed an appeal and a revisional application cannot be a ground, in the facts of the present case, for refusing to exercise the court's power under section 561A CrPC." 

 8. On reading of the provision of section 561A CrPC and the judgment of the Appellate Division quoted above, we are of the view that inherent jurisdiction of the High Court Division which is generally exercised for preventing the abuse of the process of the court in respect of the pending proceeding can also be invoked in appropriate cases for securing the ends of justice in respect of a proceeding which has reached its finality after the conclusion of trial when it is absolutely necessary to do so to secure the ends of justice. But it is necessary to keep it mind that this power is to be exercised sparingly only when the court feels it to be exercised for the ends of justice. In the case out of which the present Miscellaneous case has arisen the petitioner has been convicted not for the recovery of wrist watches and other articles alleged to have been seized but for the alleged recovery and seizure of gold from his possession which has been categorically denied by the defence. In order to arrive at the finding of guilt against the accused petitioner about illegal possession of gold the burden of the prosecution was to get the seized gold tested by expert and also to produce the gold before the court but the gold was never produced in the court for the identification by the PWs and visual inspection by the court. The prosecution has failed to discharge its burden in not producing the gold in the Court and in not furnishing any explanation for its non-production. In the case of Rouf Mia alias Rup Miah reported in 40 DLR 348 a single Bench of our High Court found with disapproval the non-production of seized articles before the court and disposal of the same during trial without obtaining permission from the court. In the present case non production of seized gold before the court without furnishing any explanation whatsoever has not only caused serious prejudice to the defence but has rendered the prosecution case highly doubtful. In total ignorance of these vital omissions amounting to lacuna and defect of the prosecution the learned trial Court has arrived at the finding of guilt of the accused petitioner which has occasioned a failure of justice. 

 9. In the case of Subal Chandra Saha vs, MS Huq, Magistrate, 1st Class, Comilla and others reported in 12 DLR 220 it was held: "A conviction based on no evidence can be quashed by a writ of certiorari." In the case of Vijai Pal and another vs. State reported in AIR 1959 (All.) 559 it was held: "The Judge hearing the represented appeal had ample powers under section 561A to prevent the abuse of the process of the court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice." In the case of Mohammad Wasi and another vs. State reported in AIR 1951 (AU.) 441 it was held that the court may and is bound to review its own order and modify or set aside an order to secure the ends of justice." In the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67 in paragraphs 8 and 10 the learned Judges of the Appellate Division endorsed the view taken earlier by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 45 DLR (AD) 175 reiterating that the power may be exercised to quash the proceeding or even a conviction on conclusion of a trial, if the court concerned got no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any criminal offence or the conviction has been based on no evidence or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The preponderance of judicial decision are that finding of guilt of accused person cannot be based merely on high probabilities but should be rested surely and firmly on the evidence and mere conjecture and hypothesis cannot take the place of proof. The learned Advocate for the accused petitioner while reading out some excerpts from the Constitutional Law of Bangladesh by Mahmudul Islam at page 395 and 398 referred to the case reported in AIR 1960 (SC) and 12 DLR 220 wherein it is observed "No evidence does not mean only dearth of evidence. It extends to any case where the evidence, taken as a whole, is not reasonably capable of supporting the finding" In the Administrative Law (HWR WADE) expression has been made to the effect that perverse and unreasonable action is unauthorized and ultra vires and where the findings are based on no satisfactory evidence there is abuse of power and may cause injustice. Thus from the laws cited above we are of the opinion that High Court Division got the power in its inherent jurisdiction to quash or set aside the judgment and order of conviction and sentence which is based on no evidence but merely on probabilities occasioning failure of justice. 

 10. In the present case the non-production of seized gold for which no explanation has been furnished by the prosecution, failure of the prosecution to test the seized gold by an expert are sufficient to show that the judgment and order of conviction is based on surmises and not on evidence and hence liable to be quashed. The prosecution case has got a rude shock when the socks, shoes and anklet which were alleged to have been seized as alamats along with the gold alleged to have been recovered from inside the said wearing of the accused petitioner, were produced before the court but the prosecution witnessess not only failed to identify those as belonging to the accused petitioner but on demonstration those were found to be much smaller in size and did not fit in the legs and feet of the accused petitioner. The prosecution case of recovery of gold from underneath the socks and anklet has thus become unreliable. 

 11. In the case before us we find that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the charge of smuggling gold against the accused petitioner and the learned court committed grave error of law in passing the order of conviction and sentence which is based on no evidence. 

 13. In the result, the Miscellaneous Case under section 56lA of the Code of Criminal Procedure succeeds and the order of conviction and sentence passed against the accused petitioner in Special Tribunal Case No. 113 of 1986 arising out of Cantonment Police Station Case No. 15(3) 86 under the Special Powers Act is hereby quashed and set aside. 

 Let the accused petitioner be set at liberty forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case. The order of confiscation of seized articles including the seized gold by the trial Court is maintained.
